🚨 ERLANG/OTP CRITICAL — TLS 1.3 CLIENT SKIPS SERVER AUTHENTICATION ON UNSOLICITED PSK  Erlang/OTP has published a critical security advisory for CVE-2026-89422: a TLS 1.3 client flaw where an unsolicited ServerHello pre_shared_key extension can make ssl:connect succeed without Certificate / CertificateVerify checks.  • Severity: Critical — CVSS 9.3 (CVSS:4.0) • GHSA: GHSA-rgxr-4g4w-j875 • Affected: OTP >= 22.2 until patched (default TLS 1.3 clients with verify_peer) • Impact: full server impersonation / MITM — attacker can hold traffic keys • Patched: OTP 29.1.1, 28.5.0.7, 27.3.4.18 (ssl 11.7.7 / 11.6.0.6 / 11.2.12.13) • Workaround until patched: restrict clients to TLS 1.2 (no TLS 1.3-safe configuration) • Credits: Milad Nasr and Luna Tong (Anthropic)  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  This is an official Erlang/OTP GitHub Security Advisory published September 22, 2026. Any application or platform using Erlang/OTP’s ssl client for TLS 1.3 with default verify_peer behavior should treat patching as urgent.  A same-day High companion advisory (GHSA-qhcm-px9c-rvfh) covers SSH session channel exhaustion DoS after authentication and ships on the same patch trains — footnote only; the lead is the TLS 1.3 client auth skip.  Official advisory: github.com/erlang/otp/securi… #DDW #DarkWeb #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #Erlang #OTP #TLS

🚨 Z.AI DISABLES ZCODE FEATURES AFTER CODING AGENT UPLOADED LOCAL GIT REPOSITORIES TO THE CLOUD  Z.ai has disabled parts of its ZCode AI coding assistant after developers discovered that the desktop agent could package and upload local code repositories — including Git history — to cloud infrastructure without clear user consent.  • The behavior was traced to ZCode’s “Codebase Indexing” / repository snapshot functionality • Z.ai acknowledged the feature had been enabled by default during the product’s early launch period • Researcher Ferstar reverse-engineered the client after finding a 313 MB encrypted archive containing a commercial project and its Git history queued for upload • Because Git history can retain old secrets, internal hostnames, deleted code and abandoned branches, the exposure can extend beyond the current working tree • Z.ai says the issue has been fixed, affected cloud data was deleted and was not used for model training • The company says independent checks by CAICT and NSFOCUS found the relevant cloud storage in a zero-data/deleted state • Z.ai has now open-sourced ZCode and says it will establish an ongoing vulnerability-reporting and response process • ZCode’s official changelog lists a fix for “abnormal repository wiki uploads” in version 3.14.0  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  AI coding agents operate inside one of the most sensitive trust zones in an organization: developer workstations and source repositories.  A feature described as “indexing” crossing the local-to-cloud boundary by default is a useful warning for enterprises deploying coding agents. Security teams need visibility not only into what models can execute, but exactly what local files, Git history, credentials and project metadata agents are permitted to transmit externally.  Original researcher analysis: blog.ferstar.org/en/posts/zc…  Official ZCode changelog: zcode.z.ai/en/changelog #ZCode #ZAI #AISecurity #CodingAgent #SourceCode #DataSecurity #AgenticAI #CyberSecurity #DDW #DarkWeb

🚨 FIRST REPORTED AUTONOMOUS AI C2 MALWARE IMPLANT DISCOVERED  Cisco Talos has disclosed CLOSEDQUORUM, what researchers believe is the first publicly documented Windows malware implant that delegates tactical command-and-control decisions directly to multiple commercial AI models.  • The malware can query DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Google Gemini • Models independently vote on what the malware should do next • The winning decision is automatically executed without continued human operator commands • Capabilities include LSASS credential dumping, browser-password theft and crypto-wallet collection • It supports process injection, persistence, ETW telemetry suppression and sandbox-evasion techniques • Stolen information can be encrypted and exfiltrated through Discord webhooks • Instead of relying solely on traditional attacker-controlled C2 logic, the implant uses legitimate LLM-provider endpoints as part of its decision architecture • Talos linked development artifacts to an individual associated with criminal-forum carding activity dating back to 2025  ⚠️ Important:  Talos has NOT confirmed deployment of CLOSEDQUORUM in the wild. The publicly analyzed build contains placeholder API keys and a dummy webhook, so this should currently be treated as emerging offensive tooling rather than an active malware campaign.  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  The architectural shift is significant: AI is no longer simply helping an attacker write malware — the models themselves are being placed inside the malware's operational decision loop.  Original Cisco Talos research: blog.talosintelligence.com/t… #AI #Malware #C2 #ThreatIntel #CyberSecurity #AgenticAI #DDW #DarkWeb

🚨 D-LINK DIR-822A CRITICAL FLAW — UNAUTH STACK OVERFLOW VIA DHCP (CVE-2026-86296), PUBLIC POC, NO PATCH YET  D-Link has published security bulletin SAP10516 for a critical stack-based buffer overflow in the DIR-822A (Non-US) router’s udhcpcd DHCP component, and says a public proof-of-concept has been reported. No firmware fix is available yet — status remains Under Investigation.  • CVE-2026-86296 — CVSS 10.0 Critical (vendor-cited CVE scoring) • Product: DIR-822A firmware A_101 (Non-US); hardware revision still under confirmation • Flaw: unbounded strcpy in udhcpcd/serverpacket.c while parsing DHCP / TR-111 Option 125 • Unauthenticated, no user interaction; network attack vector per the CVE record • Successful exploitation may cause memory corruption and can impact confidentiality, integrity, and availability (crash or potential RCE on the device) • Public PoC reported; D-Link has not released a security update as of the 21 Sep 2026 bulletin update • Same bulletin also tracks a second DIR-822A issue under investigation: CVE-2026-86510 (L2TP tunnel_set_params out-of-bounds write) • Researcher credit: tian (acknowledged by D-Link)  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  DHCP parsing is typically reachable from the LAN / adjacent segment (including guest or open Wi-Fi), so internet-wide remote exposure may be lower than a raw AV:N CVSS string suggests — but any untrusted device on the same broadcast domain can still reach the service.  This is an official vendor acknowledgement of an unpatched critical router flaw with a reported public PoC, not confirmation of mass in-the-wild exploitation. Confirm exact model, hardware revision, and firmware before acting; install only D-Link firmware intended for that revision when a fix ships.  Until then: keep the device off unnecessary internet exposure, restrict remote management, and limit who can hit the LAN DHCP path.  Original D-Link security bulletin (SAP10516): supportannouncement.us.dlink… #DLink #DIR822A #CVE202686296 #RouterSecurity #ZeroDay #IoT #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntel #DDW #DarkWeb

🚨 BIGCOMMERCE MERCHANTS HIT THROUGH COMPROMISED THIRD-PARTY RIBON APP KEY  A third-party integration compromise has exposed shopper data and allowed malicious script injection across BigCommerce merchant storefronts.  • BigCommerce confirmed credentials belonging to Ribon and Ribon 1.5 were compromised • Attackers used the legitimate third-party app access to reach merchant environments between September 13–17 • BigCommerce says malicious scripts were injected into a small number of merchant storefronts • Affected retailer Master of Malt confirmed exposed data included customer names, email addresses, phone numbers and shipping addresses • BigCommerce says account passwords and payment-card information were stored separately and were not exposed • The platform itself was NOT breached; the access path was the compromised application credential held by Ribon • BigCommerce uninstalled the affected apps to revoke attacker access and is providing logs for the developer’s investigation • The total number of affected merchants and shoppers remains unknown  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  This is a useful example of SaaS supply-chain blast radius: attackers did not need to compromise each merchant individually. Compromising a trusted integration credential created an authorized path into multiple customer environments and even enabled storefront code injection. On a recent Incident response case, we encountered VMkatz.  "It extracts Windows secrets - NTLM hash

sample_tweets.text: If your Conditional Access strategy is based on blocking users from accessing specific resources, it is not as effective as you think it is  There are hundreds of resources that are pre-consented to the scopes you are trying to block  This is the only place they are documented 👇

On a recent Incident response case, we encountered VMkatz.  "It extracts Windows secrets - NTLM hashes, DPAPI master keys, Kerberos tickets, cached domain credentials, LSA secrets, NTDS.dit, BitLocker keys - directly from VM memory snapshots and virtual disks, on the NAS, the hypervisor, wherever the VM files are." [1]  Defender detected it with the following signature: VirTool:Win64/Vekesz.A  The out-of-the-box release from the GitHub page is also heavily flagged, but one could compile (and obfuscate) the code to stay under the radar. In our case, the attacker just disabled real-time monitoring and added an exclusion:  Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "C:\"  And then pointing it to a directory, "and let it find everything", as pointed out in the documentation.  ./vmkatz.exe C:\ClusterStorage\CSV01\node-002\  I think monitoring for AV alerts (and exclusions!) could go a long way. The basics make the difference. ☝️  [1] github.com/nikaiw/VMkatz

If someone runs an eval that costs millions in compute, an agent takes a detour out of the sandbox, and now millions of dollars of compute are pointed at hacking you, I have bad news without LLMs, if someone was willing to spend millions targeting you, they were probably getting in. This has always been the dilemma with nation states like China. If someone can dramatically outspend you, well…  I realize there’s a separate argument around local models and agents, but I see leadership at all kinds of companies suddenly trying to defend against whatever swarm scenario matches the latest high profile incident.  You should probably worry more about someone pointing a 27B local model at your home built, public facing web apps than the first scenario.

I need to make a confession:  The year was 2018 and @SwiftOnSecurity was on a warpath of shower head recommendations. I had recently started a big boy job in IT and was getting paid “grown up money” for working at a help desk.  One night while checking the infosec twittersphere, I stumbled across a post that Tay made about the Delta H2OKinetic In2ition 5-in-1 shower head.  Now at this point, i’d been following Tay for 6-7 years and seen many a cyber post that built my trust in Tay’s knowledge and ability to critically think. I thought “I mean, if it sucks, I can always return it.”  Dear reader, we still have that shower head and it has been with us across state lines, multiple houses, through the raising of a now 4yo child and many washes of a dog who likes to roll in atrocious things in the wild. It’s a quality product and I am glad I bought it on a whim off a Tay shitpost about shower heads.   The moral of the story is this: if @SwiftOnSecurity recommends ANYTHING, it’s likely worth your time.
